raw_comment: I wasn’t surprised by the results of this graph. I expected almost all the sales to drop down except for online retailers like Amazon, eBay, doordash etcetera.  What interested me is that gardening sales increased. I believe this is happening because it gives people something to do during these strange times plus they don’t have to go to grocery stores as much. Another thing that I didn’t expect to plummet in sales was sports equipment. Most sports leagues are being shut down due to the virus, but I think people would buy more equipment because they are bored from being inside all day. My little cousin Tyler was really getting into basketball before the virus hit. He was so excited to play and then it was cancelled. This left him super bored with nothing to do so his parents went out and bought his own basketball and goal for himself to play in this driveway. This is what I expected most parents would do so their kid isn’t constantly nagging in their ear about being bored.

raw_comment:
This graph clearly shows how the American economy changed during the pandemic. In fact, the first thing that stands out is the increasing in sales of the nonstore retailers, but since it was all closed due to lockdown, people had to buy things from the online stores rather than than the physical shops. 
As we can see, american people bought mostly building materials and clothing perhaps because they had time to change their houses and wardrobes, since it is difficult to devote time on it .
I wonder why people have bought less things as sporting goods or hobbies, because as far as I am concerned these things have been fundamental during my quarantine period. 
Moreover, we can clearly notice that there has been an increase in sales of food services and drink places, maybe because after the restrictions people were more likely to eat in places they could not attend before.
In conclusion, the economic situation in Italy is worrying, because there are lots of cases everyday and the numbers reach those of the quarantine. We cannot allow another lockdown, otherwise we will be in danger for the balance of our economy.

1. When viewing this graph, the main thing that I notice is that it is extremely hard to comprehend and understand. Although I can see the changes in retail sales, I feel as if I have a very difficult time grasping the contents of the graph. However, after a solid viewing session of said graph, I noticed that in the previous month there was a HUGE increase in the sale of food service/drink places. I also noticed that there was a huge increase in clothing and gas station sales.

2. To be quite honest, I wonder what this graph is about. As I said before it was extremely hard for me to comprehend this graph due to the organization of the data. If I can look past the difficulty of viewing the graph, I would say that I wonder why there is such a difference in several of the main categories of retail [clothing, food, gas stations, and sporting goods]. I wonder if the pandemic is the reason for said difference or if there are other extenuating circumstances that affect the sale of certain goods and services.

3. This graph, although hard to read, has a decent impact on my community and me personally because I believe that I--along with members of my community--almost fall directly into the categories of this graph. I know that I have spent a significant less amount of time and money on goods and services now compared to a year ago. I believe that the pandemic has significantly impacted the way the worlds spends their money.

raw_comment:
It's interesting many of the increases or decreases in August retail sales from the previous year can be tied to the pandemic. For example, online shopping (nonstore retailers) has gained significant popularity. Also, it's worth looking into how many layers this data has. If just the "total retail sales" were being considered, the increase wouldn't be as prominent, but taking a step back from the bigger picture allows you to see the layers. Looking at the electronics/appliances category makes me wonder if we're seeing just the bigger picture for the technology grouping. I would've expected people to be buying more electronics (specifically more personal devices such as phones, laptops, TVs, etc) during this time, but the first graph shows a slight decrease. 

Taking all of these factors into account makes me think about how my community might have been affected. For instance, many food service/drink places and gas stations have seen a significant decrease in sales when compared to the previous year. It makes me wonder how local restaurants or gas stations have been doing these past few months. 

Headline: 
Global Pandemic: How Consumer Spending Has Changed in the US

dependency_graph.sentence: I believe that the COVID-19 pandemic is the most obvious and most likely reason for this increase.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because 'this increase' in B refers to the rise stated in A. (2) Inferential because B proposes a causal explanation for A rather than merely elaborating the statistic or expressing a separate reaction.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Proposes a cause for the observed increase, making it explanatory inference.

dependency_graph.sentence: This impacts my community and me.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B follows from the pandemic explanation in A and states a consequence for the speaker's community. (2) Inferential because it extends the causal chain to a personal/community effect rather than adding detail or a judgment.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 3: Self/community reference makes it personal/episodic.

dependency_graph.sentence: Because of the pandemic, it is important that we all stay safe and healthy.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B is a normative response to the pandemic explanation in A. (2) Evaluative because 'it is important' expresses a value judgment/prescription, not a factual consequence or elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: Although causal, the main function is normative advice about staying safe and healthy, which is prescriptive.

dependency_graph.sentence: Because of the pandemic, it is important that we all have the resources and methods to ensure this.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B continues the same normative concern by specifying what is needed to stay safe and healthy. (2) Elaborative because it refines the prior prescription rather than introducing a new causal claim or contrast.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: The sentence recommends ensuring resources and methods, functioning as a prescriptive call to action.

dependency_graph.sentence: Citizens in many places across the country are required to wear a mask in public.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B gives a concrete policy/example consistent with the safety concern in A. (2) Inferential because it presents a practical consequence/response to the pandemic rather than merely elaborating the wording of A.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Are required to' is a deontic operator prescribing behavior.

dependency_graph.sentence: Citizens in many places across the country are asked to wash their hands with soap.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B is another concrete safety measure tied to the concern in A. (2) Inferential because it states an action that follows from the need to stay safe, not just a detail of A.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Are asked to' functions as a recommendation/prescription for action.

dependency_graph.sentence: Citizens in many places across the country are asked to use hand sanitizer.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B is another concrete safety measure tied to the concern in A. (2) Inferential because it presents a recommended response to the pandemic rather than a refinement of A.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Are asked to' is a prescriptive recommendation.

dependency_graph.sentence: People are buying large amounts of whatever they think is necessary to ensure their health and safety.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B explains the increase in health and personal care sales by describing consumer behavior during the pandemic. (2) Inferential because it offers a causal mechanism, not a mere restatement or subjective reaction.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: General claim about consumer behavior, not a direct chart observation or causal explanation.

dependency_graph.sentence: The pandemic brought more awareness to people about their hygiene.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B gives a reason for the increase in A by linking the pandemic to hygiene awareness. (2) Inferential because it is an explanatory claim about why the increase happened.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Attributes increased awareness to the pandemic, which is causal explanation.

dependency_graph.sentence: The pandemic brought more awareness to people about how to keep up with their hygiene.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B restates the hygiene-awareness idea from A with slightly different wording. (2) Elaborative because it refines the same point rather than adding a new cause, judgment, or contrast.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Explains the awareness increase as caused by the pandemic.

dependency_graph.sentence: These reasons support the increase in sales in this category.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because 'these reasons' refers to the pandemic-related explanations given earlier for the increase in A. (2) Inferential because B draws a conclusion from those reasons, rather than simply elaborating the increase or expressing a stance.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Explicitly links reasons to the observed increase, making it explanatory.

dependency_graph.sentence: I wonder if there will be a decline in sales once the pandemic is over.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B is a speculative question prompted by the increase in A. (2) Evaluative because it expresses curiosity about a future outcome rather than a factual explanation or elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 5: Explicit curiosity about a future decline.

dependency_graph.sentence: I wonder if there will be a decline in sales once a cure is found.

depends_on.justification: (1) Edge exists because B is a parallel future-oriented question to A, differing only in the condition (a cure). (2) Elaborative because it extends the same curiosity in a closely related way rather than introducing a new stance or causal claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 5: Explicit curiosity about a hypothetical future decline.

raw_comment: Analyzing the data provided by the chart above, it is undoubtedly noticeable in which sectors Americans invested most of their money. In July 2020, during the pandemic, it is clear how people have chosen to devote themselves to personal care and that of their homes, as the categories of healthcare, furniture and building materials/ garden have experienced an increase in sales. This makes me imagine that families wanted to reorganize their spaces so as to change the atmosphere of their houses and then to spend money on clothing and furniture, rather than shop on some other thinks  like sporting goods/ hobbies/musical instruments/ books/, which instead was a decreasing economic sector. I really wonder how it is possible, since during my quarantine period, I did nothing but reading or devote myself to my hobbies, like work out or painting. Another thing that surprised me was seeing how this year there was a sharp increase in food services/drink places sales, but I guess it is because a lot of people, after the lockdown period, decided to try new places to meet with friends or work colleagues. However, the situation in the United States makes me wonder which economic sectors in my country have experienced an increase or decrease in sales, as the current situation is quite serious for the economy of Italy: cases of covid-19 are increasing and people choose to save their money in view of a possible second lockdown.

raw_comment:
Title: How economy changed throughout the pandemic.
I looked very closely at this graph and I noticed the decrease of consumer spending in certain economic sectors. If we pay attention to the percentages, we can sefely say that consumers tended to spend money on superficial objects (such as building materials) rather than clothes and such. This pandemic really influenced our priorities: the percentages of clothes, food services and drink places increased considerably (even though there was a restriction, so I find it really odd), while the percentages of building materials and sporting goods decreased drastically. It’s really easy to understand why: gyms had to close due to a restriction, so people could not invest in sport supplies.
I wonder if the economy will keep changing, if other sectors will be revalued, if the new priorities will remain such, for example masks, sanitizers and body care (whose percentage surprisingly has not increased as drastically as I expected).
This problem doesn't concern me personally, as none of my family works in a sector that isn't as important now as it was last year. However I can say with certainty that the community, has been very conditioned: many workers lost their jobs or their wages were reduced.
I personally think this graphic made me actually realized the whole situation in America: how the economy was changing, the consequences, which sector was getting the most attention during the pandemic and what the new priorities have become.

raw_comment:
Title: How economy changed throughout the pandemic.
I looked very closely at this graph and I noticed the decrease of consumer spending in certain economic sectors. If we pay attention to the percentages, we can sefely say that consumers tended to spend money on superficial objects (such as building materials) rather than clothes and such. This pandemic really influenced our priorities: the percentages of clothes, food services and drink places increased considerably (even though there was a restriction, so I find it really odd), while the percentages of building materials and sporting goods decreased drastically. It’s really easy to understand why: gyms had to close due to a restriction, so people could not invest in sport supplies.
I wonder if the economy will keep changing, if other sectors will be revalued, if the new priorities will remain such, for example masks, sanitizers and body care (whose percentage surprisingly has not increased as drastically as I expected).
This problem doesn't concern me personally, as none of my family works in a sector that isn't as important now as it was last year. However I can say with certainty that the community, has been very conditioned: many workers lost their jobs or their wages were reduced.
I personally think this graphic made me actually realized the whole situation in America: how the economy was changing, the consequences, which sector was getting the most attention during the pandemic and what the new priorities have become.

raw_comment:
Title: How economy changed throughout the pandemic.
I looked very closely at this graph and I noticed the decrease of consumer spending in certain economic sectors. If we pay attention to the percentages, we can sefely say that consumers tended to spend money on superficial objects (such as building materials) rather than clothes and such. This pandemic really influenced our priorities: the percentages of clothes, food services and drink places increased considerably (even though there was a restriction, so I find it really odd), while the percentages of building materials and sporting goods decreased drastically. It’s really easy to understand why: gyms had to close due to a restriction, so people could not invest in sport supplies.
I wonder if the economy will keep changing, if other sectors will be revalued, if the new priorities will remain such, for example masks, sanitizers and body care (whose percentage surprisingly has not increased as drastically as I expected).
This problem doesn't concern me personally, as none of my family works in a sector that isn't as important now as it was last year. However I can say with certainty that the community, has been very conditioned: many workers lost their jobs or their wages were reduced.
I personally think this graphic made me actually realized the whole situation in America: how the economy was changing, the consequences, which sector was getting the most attention during the pandemic and what the new priorities have become.

raw_comment:
Title: How the pandemic affected the US everyday expenses
Observing the graph I noticed is that the sales from the nonstore retailers remained the same as last years, while the sporting goods/hobbies/musical instruments decreased, and it surprises me, since during a quarantine there isn't much to do and it would have been the perfect time to master new hobbies or read books, but probably they chose to save money to spend on more useful things like groceries or sanitary products.
I wonder why the health/personal care products didn't increase considering that we are in the middle of a global pandemic and our health should be the most important thing to us right now.
This graph shows how during times like these the economy completely changed, and how obviously it also affects me and my community. In fact a lot of restaurants and small businesses had to shut their activities down during the pandemic since no one could go out and their sales decreased so much they couldn't be able to gain anymore from their activity, and also a lot of people lost their job since the owners of the activities could not afford to pay them.

raw_comment:
United States pandemic through economy’s eyes.

Watching the graph, I noticed how the pandemic influenced the request of the consumers, changing from general objects to first necessities like food and drinks. We can see how the request for food, drinks and clothing increased and at the same time the request for motor vehicles part and general merchandise decreased. I noticed also that the non stores retailers’ request stayed the same, probably because the restrictions due to the Covid pandemic did not affect that type of business at all. 
In my surprise I noticed that the gas station business didn’t collapse as, for example, the sporting goods and hobbies did. It made me wonder how can this be possible considering the emergency measurement and the lockdown. People were not allowed to leave their houses so I was expecting them to spend more time in new or past hobbies, health or self-care, which was another decreasing economic sector. I think this graph made me more aware of how the global pandemic influenced the United States’ economy and people’s life. It made me also wonder what if in Italy happened the same during the three months of lockdown. 
After reading and analysing the graph I can say that I am now definitely more concerned about what might happen to Italy’s economy if there will be a second lockdown considering that the United States business went through such complicacy even though the country has one of the strongest economies globally.

raw_comment: I noticed that there is an increase in so many retail sales this August as compared to last summer. I was under the impression that the economy was suffering more drastically as a result of the pandemic, and I'm sure it was during earlier months and more intense quarantine, however, total retail sales have gone up 2.6% compared with last August. It makes sense that there was a big increase in sales for gardening materials, hobbies, and health care, however, some of the other increases in spending surprised me and I was additionally surprised that some of the decrease percentages aren't higher. I wonder how May 2019 and May 2020 would compare because this was the peak of quarantine and I would be interested to see how much total retail was down. This impacts me because it shows me that although certain industries as striving, many businesses are also struggling financially as a result of the virus. Local businesses struggling affects the whole community. A more personal impact is that gas prices have greatly decreased, allowing me to save money. Potential title: The Pandemic's Effect on our Economy, both Local and National

raw_comment:
Title: the change in America’s economy
The first thing that I noticed is that Americans kept using nonstore retailers during quarantine, even though i thought that there could have been an increase considered that during quarantine people could not do groceries as before, so that they’d use more online shopping.
A thing that surprised me is that in July 2020 people didn’t consume as much as they did in August 2019 on personal care, considered that in a period of emergency like this maybe the personal care should be our first concern.
While a thing that didn’t surprise me was the decrease in sporting goods/hobbies/musical instruments/books because I think that a lot of people had to save the money in order to maintain the family, so it’s very understandable.
I really wonder how is it possible that sectors like drink places and gas stations have totally changed direction, weighed that during pandemic there has been a lot of restrictions.
Seeing this graph made me think about how the economy sector changed, and how this whole situation had a great impact on me and especially on my community.
A lot of small stores had to close or reduce the days off in order to gain more money. And I also imagine that many stores had to close because for a manager could be very hard to give a salary to each worker when they had to close the store for a long period.
I think that graphs like this help a lot to understand which sectors are economically in difficulty as a consequence of the pandemic.

raw_comment:
Looking at this graph the first thing I noticed is that the category Nonstore retailers is the only one that hasn’t changed. I also noted the decrease in sales as regards food/drinks stations while the categories food services, motor vehicles/ parts and gas stations are increased. It seemed rather strange to me and I wondered how it was possible since the restrictions caused by the covid.  
However I was not surprised by the percentage increase regarding health/ personal care and building materials/garden. 
Subsequently I wondered why the sector hobbies is decreased since, at least as far as I am concerned, I used my time during the pandemic to read books or play the guitar. Later I pondered why this graph had been made and in my opinion the purpose is understand which sectors need the most help from the State. 
Lastly looking these percentages made me think about my community. I was somewhat worried because probably my country is in the same condition if not worse and it made me immediately think that if there had to be a new lockdown, Italy would be seriously ruined.

title: Americans in quarantine. 
Looking at this graph made me better understood how Americans have spent their quarantine. It is noticeable how specific categories of objects have been more shopped: books, health/personal care things, gardening tools and many other objects have increased their sale. This is a clear consequence of Americans having more time to dedicate to their selves and their houses. In fact, clothing sales, restaurants and gas stations have suffered heavy losses compared to last year due to people staying at home. However I wonder if and when this sectors will manage to significantly rise in sales in order to overcome the crisis. I am sure my country is in a similar situation and that is why being quarantined again really scares me.

raw_comment:
The changes between August 2019 and August 2020 are reflective of the U.S.'s transition into quarantine. The drastic increase in nonstore retailers (which do not require a person to physically leave their homes in order to purchase goods) and materials for homes, hobbies, and creativity demonstrate that Americans spent their time inside. Many people ate indoors, marked by the reduced sales at restaurants and other food/drink locations. A decrease in travel can be inferred by the drop in gas station sales. While there is virtually no change between July and August 2020 it is clear that people slowly began to abandon at home activities to indulge in in-store shopping, restaurant outings, and the like. August 2020 shows signs of the public attempting to return to some semblance of normalcy. To my curiosity, electronics/appliances retail sales did not experience as much change as other retail forms. While many of these results make sense conceptually on a larger scale, I do not see my specific community yielding results this dramatic (except for maybe in the food/drink places section). This causes me to wonder what (if any) communities had the greatest effects on the data presented.

Possible Headline: Staying Home Makes an Economy Lazy

raw_comment:
When looking at this graph, a couple things are noticeable right away. The first being that Nonstore retailers is the only category that experienced no change in retail sales from the previous month. I also noticed that the things that one my expect to increase with the pandemic such as building materials/garden and sporting goods/hobbies/musical instruments/books increased. On the same thought, those categories that one might expect to decrease such as clothing, gas stations, and food service-drink places decreased. 
I wonder why some of the numerical data is presented as a percentage while the majority are just normal numbers. I also wonder what would fall under nonstore retailers as I would imagine this includes online shopping among other things.

In regards to my community, I think this graphic might help people to understand how exactly this pandemic has affected different fields of retail and possibly encourage them to support retail fields that may be struggling right now.

I think that most of the categories that had more sales such as food service, furniture,  electronics, and clothing had more sales because over the pandemic people had a lot of takeout, had time to update their houses with new furniture,  needed to get electronics for their zoom meetings, and had time to online shop. I wonder why the gas stations had an increase of sales even when people are not driving places as much as they used to. This graph has a huge impact on our community because people who work in the places who are losing sales could lose their jobs and many stores would be closing which would be bad for the whole community. A headline for this graph could be: How the Pandemic Affected Sales

raw_comment:
The graph expresses exactly what is important to the people in the middle of a health crisis. As people cannot go out for a long amount of time, nonstore retailers like amazon and other online stores able to maintain, not increase their retail sales. On the other hand, things that do not affect the wellbeing of the people like sports good, music instrument, books have a decrease in retail sales. 

What do you wonder? 
It is very interesting to see an increase in both food service and gas stations. While food service/drink places  decrease in retail price, food/drink stores increase in retail price. The gas situation is also quite hard to understand especially when everyone is supposed to stay at home, be in lock down, and do not need to use their cars as much.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Because of the huge change in consumer spending, the economy was not in a very good situation at the beginning of the pandemic. However, as people started to get use to things, they were able to use a lot of what is happening to their advantage and bring the economy back to normal.

raw_comment:
The graph expresses exactly what is important to the people in the middle of a health crisis. As people cannot go out for a long amount of time, nonstore retailers like amazon and other online stores able to maintain, not increase their retail sales. On the other hand, things that do not affect the wellbeing of the people like sports good, music instrument, books have a decrease in retail sales. 

What do you wonder? 
It is very interesting to see an increase in both food service and gas stations. While food service/drink places  decrease in retail price, food/drink stores increase in retail price. The gas situation is also quite hard to understand especially when everyone is supposed to stay at home, be in lock down, and do not need to use their cars as much.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Because of the huge change in consumer spending, the economy was not in a very good situation at the beginning of the pandemic. However, as people started to get use to things, they were able to use a lot of what is happening to their advantage and bring the economy back to normal.

raw_comment:
The graph expresses exactly what is important to the people in the middle of a health crisis. As people cannot go out for a long amount of time, nonstore retailers like amazon and other online stores able to maintain, not increase their retail sales. On the other hand, things that do not affect the wellbeing of the people like sports good, music instrument, books have a decrease in retail sales. 

What do you wonder? 
It is very interesting to see an increase in both food service and gas stations. While food service/drink places  decrease in retail price, food/drink stores increase in retail price. The gas situation is also quite hard to understand especially when everyone is supposed to stay at home, be in lock down, and do not need to use their cars as much.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Because of the huge change in consumer spending, the economy was not in a very good situation at the beginning of the pandemic. However, as people started to get use to things, they were able to use a lot of what is happening to their advantage and bring the economy back to normal.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the products and areas of merchandise that are receiving an increase in sales than last year are the ones the are targeted towards home improvement and staying entertained at home. Meanwhile, the industries that are declining are the ones that require the consumers to be out of the house and moving around. 
2. I wonder what types of businesses and products fall under the miscellaneous category. I'm also curious to see how these statistics have evolved with the start of school and having students, teachers, and parents out of the house more often and requiring more things. 
3. A possible impact this could have on me is how much money I make in my high school job. I work in the clothing department of Target, and during the initial quarantine it was extremely clear that clothes were not the priority to consumers. Most shifts, I was switched to other departments because of the lack of activity on the sales floor. Sales have picked up again, but I was shocked to see how far behind clothing retail sales were in August. Consumers not purchasing clothes affects how many shifts are available for me to work, and therefore how much money I am able to earn. 
4. A catchy headline could be "Corona Consumers".

Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  “Retail Spending, Featuring Covid-19” by Elizabeth in St. Paul, Minnesota; “Covid Killing Retailers” by Ivan of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, North Carolina; “Coivd sales not what you expected!” by Sophie in Massachusetts; “Rising Retail During ‘Rona: Total August 2020 retail sales increase in comparison to the previous year” by Lauren of AOSE; and "Are Clothing Stores Dying? What Else Has Crashed in 2020?" by Sarah of Claremont High School in Claremont, California

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back on Friday, Oct. 16 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that there is a significant change in consumer spending involving food service/drink places, clothing, hobbies, sporting goods, building materials, and furnishing in the month of August compared to last year. Many of these make sense due to the pandemic. For example food services most likely went up in August because this is when places started to open back up from being shut down during quarantine. It also makes sense as to why the furnishing and building materials went up also. Many people renovated their homes during quarantine because they had the extra time to. Lastly, this can also be a major reason as to why the clothing sales went up in the past month.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the sporting goods/hobbies sales went down by so much from last year to this month? Maybe it can be because many people ran out of books or hobbies to try in the last month since that it is what most people were doing during quarantine. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts my community because many local businesses are struggling financially from being closed during the pandemic. It is good to see that as a community we are all making the effort to go to food services to help them recover from this.

A headline for this graph could be: 
Changes In Retail? Blame Corona.

raw_comment:
I have summarized our collective thoughts from our introductory statistics class at St. Catherine University in St. Paul, MN:

We noticed that for food/drink and clothing, sales decreased over the past year but went up over the past month. We wonder if this is because the yearlong trend reflects restaurants and stores closing during the lockdown, while over the past month things are reopening more. 

We also notice that people are spending more on sporting goods, gardening and home materials over the past year. This might be because since people need to stay home more, they might as well do productive and fun things like renovate their house and maintain gardens.

Impacts on our community: Local restaurants and retailers are struggling financially.

Catchy headline: Retail Spending, Featuring Covid-19

raw_comment: This graph provided an interesting perspective of what was going on during the pandemic. At first, some of the information seemed a little weird and inaccurate, but the more I thought about it, the more it made sense. For example, I was pretty confused when I saw that total retail sales on gas had gone up, but if you think about it, it isn't surprising at all. Airports are a lot less popular because of COVID, so people are driving when they want to travel. I traveled a lot but drove everywhere to do it and went to more isolated places. A lot of people I know did the same thing, so this stat, like some of the others on the graph, makes a lot more sense after a little analysis.  The one thing that did confuse me was the sports/hobbies/instruments category. I can understand why spending on sports went down, as practices and games were canceled, but I feel like spending on things like instruments and other materials needed for hobbies would've gone up. I know I definitely had more time for hobbies, so this was the only one that didn't really make sense to me.  Obviously, COVID has affected our way of life as a whole, but our spending habits were one of the most changed things overall.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that during the month of August 2020 (in the middle of the coronavirus pandemic), people in the United States began to spend more money in home improvement (i.e. building materials/furniture), personal improvement (hobbies/books/health), and less money in gas, food service, and clothing. The data in the graph is not surprising. It is expected that when people stay home, they spend less money in malls and gas stations. It also appears that the change in retail sales from the month of July to the month of August varied randomly within different categories, implying that the quarantine status of most individuals also did not vary.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how much the changes in retail sales have boosted some businesses and halted others. Have gas station prices decreased because of the decrease in demand? Have in-person clothing stores been filing for bankruptcy?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
With the 2020 presidential election coming up, most Americans are concerned over the impact of the pandemic on the economy. There remain many debates over Trump’s regulation of the economy during the national crisis. Trump supporters believe the success of the economy after such a detrimental historic event is proof that Trump is a good president, while Trump’s opponents argue against this claim.

raw_comment: Covid has changed the economy, comparing it to last years. I think covid defiantly changed peoples spending habits. During the beginning of quarantine, I wasn't spending as much money on food because I couldn't go out to eat with friends due to the restaurants being closed. I was not surprised to see that health/personal care went up by 0.8. I think a lot of people during the pandemic took time to better themselves. They had more time to focus on them, maybe not so much what they were going to wear to work the next day. I was surprised to see that gas stations went up by 0.4. For me I remember my mom saying how she didn't have to get gas in so long because we weren't going anywhere. But people also used this time to take road trips with friends or family. Overall I think a lot of people used this time to work on themselves and homes.

raw_comment:
Most of these changes are either expected or excusable, maybe with the exception of nonstore retailers and foodservice (I mean, really, food service? What?). What I am more concerned about is what the lasting impact of this will be. After one, two, or ten years, will the economy return to what it once was, or has covid permanently shifted it?

Personally, I have a feeling most of the changes will thin out over time, but that there will be more permanent market shifts. People get used to different things and learn what parts of the economy were going under/were not worth going up. For example, nonstore retailers and online services may go significantly higher from now on because of COVID. But that's just my guess; I could be totally wrong and nothing changes at all, or maybe the market is permanently altered/broken/renewed. There are countless possibilities.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

During March and April 2020, much of the country’s retail stores and restaurants closed down.  Consumers stopped spending in-person and went online or deferred purchases.  Slowly, stores have been reopening and shoppers have resumed shopping.  Today’s graph shows compare August 2020 sales to pre-Covid August 2019 and to the recent July 2020.  How is consumer spending different from a year ago and from the prior month?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Finally, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

By Friday, we’ll reveal the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  Reply even after you have read the Reveal.
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  Stay tuned for next week’s graph about climate threats.

raw_comment: I have noticed that the graph showing the retail sales of this past month have decreased by 2.0 percent. It makes sense that this is the cause, due to Covid-19 stores haven’t been able to hold as many people as they used to. As well as not many people going out to do simple things like shopping for their groceries or clothing. I wonder why the sports/hobbies/musical instruments/books category has gone down the most. They are struggling, but like most businesses have been doing,  they have been brainstorming new ways to continue selling their products, whether that is through better publicity or different sale methods.
A catchy headline could be: "Then and Now: Retail Sales feat. COVID"

raw_comment: This graph is showing us consumer spending in the previous year and in the previous month when corona was in full swing. I understand why most of the graph is like the way it is, for instance, I can understand why it went down last month because sports are canceled and people can’t wear things out like cleats or a new ball of some sort. The clothing has gone up because Mrs. Lucas-as a female- said that females have grown a little in the weight category and are needing new clothes. That is just a sample of what makes sense to me. The thing I don’t get, is why gas stations are going up. Last year gas stations were15.4 in sales and last month they were +0.4 in sales. Where are people going last month than in last year? Last year people had to drive to work, drop off/pick up their kid(s) at/from school run errands etc. not going out to eat because the food serves/ drink places are going up. Not going to stores because all the sails are down on the graph. Another thing that I thought that was interesting was how last year the sales went high to low. I don’t know if that means anything or is just by chance or somebody put them in that order, while last month numbers are all over the place and are not that high or low.

raw_comment:
Over the span of the whole Pandemic I have heard a lot of talk on how the economy would be impacted. This graph gives me a clearer insight on each specific category sales. You can see a clear increase in home improvement, grocery stores, health and non-store realtors. This seems to make perfect sense because people had so much extra time in their house they turned to home improvement projects or learning a new hobby. On the other hand, we can see a decrease in gas and food service/ drink places because many were staying in.

 I often think about the small and local businesses. My grandparents own a restaurant in Georgia and I know that they felt the strain covid had on their sales. They were itching to get back even though they are at a higher risk for covid because they are elderly. My mom told me that they predicted something like 1in 6 businesses would go out of business.

raw_comment:
Above is a graph comparing last year's retail sales in August to this year's retail sales in August. You can see there is a major difference in certain areas, for example: The sporting goods/ hobbies/ musical instruments/ books retail dropped 16.8% in the past year. If people are staying home all the time then you would assume the retail percentages would be at their peak in this area. 
     Food service/ drink places increased 20% in the past year, this can be because people are going out and buying food rather than cooking food, or people are supporting local businesses and buying food from there. Retail in clothing increased by 23%, this is probably due to gyms being closed and not being able to exercise properly so people are gaining weight and buying new clothes. Or it can be the opposite, people can find quarantine as a time to lose weight so they are losing weight and buying new clothes to fit themselves. 
     The community I am in has many local businesses, or main staple is local businesses. Some have had to close down because of the Coronavirus. In my town, every April, we have a festival. This is where small businesses make most of their money for the year because people from all walks of life come and buy things. But this year, the festival was canceled, they lost their biggest shot of the year to make some money. It was a struggle they would soon have to face for the rest of 2020.

raw_comment:
In 2019, non-store retail sales were considerably lower. Since we are facing a worldwide pandemic, not as many people have left their homes. As a result, establishments like restaurants, gas stations, and clothing stores have seen a decline in sales. However, nonstore retailers have seen a large increase in sales because people have more time on their hands. This virus has given people the chance to not only enjoy their old hobbies, but find some new ones. 
     Despite the positive effect this pandemic has had on nonstore retailers, a lot of local businesses have been suffering. That could mean some of my favorite restaurants and stores could shut down. The other day, I heard one of my favorite shopping centers is going close due to lack of sales. That completely broke my heart. I used to go there to shop with my friends all the time. As afraid as we are to catch Covid, it's important that we find ways to support our local businesses.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I notice that the creator chose to orient the list from greatest increase to greatest decrease over the year rather than from month to month.
Unsurprisingly, retail sales of hobby and home items have increased since August 2019, while places like gas stations, clothing stores, and restaurants have seen drops in sales. 

2. What do you wonder? 

I wonder where this data was obtained from. I also wonder why non-store retailers have a separate category while they sell similar items to other retailers. How would the graph change if this weren't the case? Lastly, why did the creator of this graph feel it would be more beneficial to compare yearly v.s. monthly?

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

Stores close to me may choose to alter their inventory as they reopen. If sales drop too much, stores (especially restaurants) may close. Stores that do not have an online presence may be forced to create a website to stay alive in a changing market.

4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Non-Store Sells More: growth of online sales in the COVID pandemic

raw_comment: I notice that in the past year, non-retail sales are up and retail sales are down. Characteristically, things that you do from home are up, like people buying bikes and gardening. Food/drink stores are also up from last year. This makes sense because restaurants haven’t been open. Overall, people are spending more money on things and activities related to their home than on things related to outside of their house. I can agree with this. My family has done a different amount of home improvement projects. However, with school starting again, I can see this changing in my day-to-day life. I wonder how businesses who are struggling are dealing with this shift in spending. I wonder how much longer home activities will be on the positive side of the graph when you can already see sporting goods/hobbies are already starting to move down and restaurants and clothing are starting to trend up. In the past week, I’ve gone clothes shopping with my mom and my dad bought some electronics to better his work space. In my own community, I know people are trying to support local restaurants because they are struggling with people not going out to eat as much. My parents both work for companies that haven’t been extraordinarily affected in the fluctuations in this economy. Due to this, we’re able to order takeout from local places, like Vito’s Pizza, which I do hope helps a little.

raw_comment:
I notice that things that give people something to do have increased in sales from last year (such as supplies for projects, hobbies, and self-care). I see that food and drink stores have increased from last year, while food service and drink places have had a huge decrease from last year. I see that sales for hobby supplies have increased from last year but decreased from this year. The opposite effect is apparent with food service, gas stations, and clothing.
I wonder whether people going back to work/school has caused a reversal in sales compared to last year and compared to last month (shown with gas stations, food service, clothing, and hobby supplies). Why were electronics and appliances down from last year? I would have expected the opposite effect because of people working and going to school at home on top of using their appliances more.
This has a huge impact on my community. The huge increase in sales from nonstore retailers has caused issues with our own small businesses. With restaurants doing so poorly in the beginning, many places where I had memories have closed.
My title for the graph would be "A Change in Extra Change: How the Coronavirus Has Impacted Consumer Spending".

raw_comment:
This graph shows the changes that the pandemic has had on stores and retails. Over the last year, non store retailers have obviously increased because people want to order online instead of having to go somewhere and a lot of places have been closed.  Building and garden materials, sporting goods, hobbies, musical instruments, and books have also increased because people have been bored over quarantine with not much to do and have figured out more of what they enjoy.  Food service, drink places, gas stations, and clothing have all decreased because restaurants and clothing stores have been closed or have changed their times to be more limited, causing less people to go out and need gas as often.  
Comparing the previous month to the previous year, you don’t see much change because honestly in our world there hasn’t been much change.  The pandemic is still going on, more restaurants and stores are open now, but most with limited times.  I think that is why you see such little change with everything in the previous month graph.

raw_comment:
I find it interesting that books, hobby supplies, and sporting goods, have actually gone down since then. You would think these would still be in high demand since we’re all still stuck at home. I also find it confounding that foodservice and drink places are still going up even with social distancing guidelines. I think it shows how people aren’t really following safety guidelines and are prolonging the pandemic. The non-store retailers and gardening supplies aren’t that surprising either since many people have stepped out of their comfort zone and begun gardening. It’s also interesting to see that clothing has also been on the rise after a large decline last year. I find it strange that the health/personal care products haven’t gone up more, as we should be taking time to take care of ourselves.
 One thing I notice is that mainly necessities seem to be on the rise. Maybe this is because people are losing their jobs at alarming rates and can only pay for the bare minimum. Thinking from that perspective makes this graph more impactful. It makes me wonder how many children will miss Christmas or their birthdays because their parents, who have previously been in a financially stable place, can barely afford to keep them fed. Their parents, who haven’t been able to take care of themselves either. There also isn’t rise or fall of over 5.7%, which is showing how our economy is a little frozen. I wonder what the graph will look like next year.

raw_comment:
How the pandemic has changed where we put our money.

I notice in this graph that there was a huge dip in sales back in 2019 for items such as food/drink, electronics, gas stations, and clothing. But back last month, there was a dip for sport supplies, and a raise in items such as food/drink, appliances, gas stations, and clothing. I wonder if this has a lot to do with the pandemic and the stimulus checks given out. Perhaps these checks are getting used by many families for non essential items. This impacts me and my community because it shows where us humans are really putting our money. Many people have been bored during the pandemic, so they’ve been spending excessively for things like clothes and appliances. Many of us are taking these stimulus checks for granted and the money is just getting pocketed at the end of the day. I like the idea of the checks, but I’m not sure everyone truly is in need of one by the look at this graph.

raw_comment: While many comments circle the ideas of retail, food, and sports equipment growth, my eyes went to the gas station statistics. Between August 2019 and August 2020, the consumer spending for gas stations has decreased 15.4%. When seeing this, I automatically think of how good it is for our environment. Sure, the economic side to the situation may be struggling, but when many other parts of our economy are thriving, I can see this as a good thing. Climate change is something that I’m worried about and take a lot of caution towards. When seeing that gas consumption has lowered, I can infer that emissions are also lowering. This is really good for our environment in a time of crisis.

raw_comment: I noticed that the sales in electronics went up which was not surprising because I figured that people likely spend more time on their computers and/or they may have bought a new one for distance learning or working from home. I also noticed that the sales in sporting goods, hobbies, music, and books went down. This is likely because less sports are being played because of the pandemic and the other stores such as book stores have likely been closed. I wonder why the gas station sales went up.  am curious about this because I would have assumed that gas station sales would have gone down because less people are driving to things such as sporting events and work. This has a negative impact on me and my community because although total retail sales are up many stores and restaurants are having to close their doors forever. For example, a restaurant near me called ¨Islands¨ recently closed. This graph is comparing retail sales in August from 2020 to 2019. Headline: COVID and the shocking business results it brings.

 I noticing some surprising and nonsupporting increase. The online stores have a explosive increase, due to everyone being at home. One that I found interesting was the gardening sales, I wonder if it is because people are very bored and feeling trapped. I wonder why hobbies have sunk so low as you think they would increase a lot more with nothing to do but I speculate that because it is grouped with sporting goods, which probably make the average a lot lower because no sports are going on right now.

raw_comment:
The statistics that stood out to me were that while consumer spending at food service/drink places, at gas stations, and for clothing had decreased a significant amount the previous year, before the pandemic, it actually increased during the pandemic. The overall trend of the graph was that before the pandemic retail sales had grown, but during the pandemic, consumer spending did not grow or change very much. These three areas were outliers, going against the trend of the graph. The increase in spending for clothing and food service/drink places during the pandemic made sense to me. Even though not as many people are going out to eat, there probably been a significant increase in the amount of people ordering delivery, and many people most likely purchased clothing because they were going back to school or work. I do wonder why spending at gas stations increased. When many people are staying at home and aren't driving as much as they usually would be, why would spending at gas stations increase?
For the most part, this graph is showing how consumer spending has decreased during the pandemic. Due to this, many small businesses in my community are struggling to stay afloat, and some have already closed. A headline that I would use for this graph is "Covid Consumerism" as the graph explains how Covid has affected consumerism.

raw_comment:
At first I was kind of confused as to why hobby items such as sporting goods and instrument sales went down. When you think about it, during this time you have a huge opportunity to take up some single person hobbies that you have been wanting to try. So why would the numbers go down this month? Well, most of the time, if you purchase quality goods for these hobbies, you don't need to but items for a while. For example, I play the flute. I don't need to get a new flute every month because flutes last long if you take care of them. So, sales are probably down, not because people lost interest, but because you don't need to buy those items as often as groceries. Just because you didn't buy something, doesn't mean you are using the same thing at home. 


Also, I wasn't surprised that gardening materials were on a rise. I say this because you have more time to tend to the plants and take care of a garden. Personally, my family started a garden during the pandemic because we wanted something new to try. Ours didn't work out too well once I started school, but many others also had the same idea. Also, if you want to support locals, check out your local plant nurseries. 

One thing that also kind of surprised me was the rise in clothing this previous month. One reason this may be is because people have either been losing or gaining weight depending on the habits they have picked up in quarantine. The only other reason I can think of would be a change in style due to media influence

raw_comment: Before the pandemic, everyone was out in restaurants, shopping etc. However, now-days, due to the pandemic, people were in their "Comfort Zone". People started to react differently and stay away from outside activities such as restaurants and shopping. For example, their reaction was to use online shopping instead of malls, and for restaurants more and more people are eating from their houses. However, their are some people in restaurants such as Fast Food restaurants. Also I am very puzzled how gas retail sales are growing considering that less and less people are going out. One catchy head line is "Dramatic Changes in Retail Sales". I also realized that Food services are going up maybe because  millions of people don't have food during the pandemic, so they are dependent on the Food Department, which is why it is going up.  To add on,more and more people are dependent on food services. I also noticed that hobbies are going down. This also puzzled me because I thought that hobbies should go up, considering that more people then before a couple months ago are at home. To add on, I also thought that more hobbies are being developed in the process during quarantine. During the Pandemic there has been a lot of changes regarding the retail sales.

This graph shows a very interesting trend: we can see that health/personal care items and building materials have grown in percentage during the pandemic, since people are now more careful to preserve their health and tend to spend their time on household chores. 
I also notice that non-store retailers have grown exponentially as people prefer to stay home more. As a matter of fact gas stations seem to have decreased, along with clothing and food services. Therefore I wonder why motor vehicles/parts have increased in sales, considering that people were supposed to stay home.
In conclusion, I could say that this graph actually represents how our lives have changed during the pandemic and it is fascinating to see what has really become important to our community during this extraordinary time, so a headline might be “ How COVID-19 has changed an average consumer’s needs”.

raw_comment:
Headline: Retail Sales in a Pandemic
In the graph, it shows how retail sales changed from last year and July compared to August. We can see that for nonstore retailers, sales went up a lot from last year, but the sales in August stayed the same from July. We can also see that total retail sales went up 2.6% from last year. Also, we can see a decrease in sales for miscellaneous items, electronics/appliances, food services/drink places, gas stations, and clothing. This is probably because a lot of people are staying inside because of the pandemic and they don't need these items as much.

Title: The Changes of The Consumer During A Global Pandemic

The graph shows the change in consumer spending on certain items/activities. I noticed that last year, people spent lots of money on their interests, hobbies, sporting goods, etc. In the previous month, people stopped purchasing those things. Instead, they began to purchase more landscaping/gardening materials and health/personal care. Nonstore retailers, such as Amazon, experienced no change. I wonder why people spent more money on gas money, since we were supposed to stay home, in lockdown.

raw_comment:
Title: The Effects of Covid-19 on Retail Sales

The Covid-19 Pandemic has had a significant effect on our economy, including retail sales. In places where it is more common for you to go in and buy things, the retail sales have gone down. Places that don't require you to do things in person as much, like nonstore retailers, have benefitted the most from this Pandemic. As well, stores that connect with common hobbies, like sporting goods stores, and music stores have benefitted, showing that the boredom that people are experiencing from being cramped up is translating into higher demand for these types of products. That is talking from the perspective of August to the previous year, but as well there is quite a bit of change in the previous month, where the stores revolving around hobbies have dropped and the ones that have been hurting have been slowly moving back to normal.
